summary: Defines xCal, an XML representation of iCalendar data. It lets calendar information that normally uses the text iCalendar format be exchanged as XML.

eli5.summary: Calendar events are usually saved in a special text style. This gives the same event information in XML, a different style that many programs find easier to handle.

questions: how to convert icalendar to xml
subtitle: A plain mapping that turns iCalendar calendar data into XML and back again without losing meaning.

tldr.problem: iCalendar is a widely used format for calendar and scheduling data, but it is specialized and needs its own parser and generator, while XML has many tools for generating, parsing and manipulating data.
tldr.mechanism: xCal maps iCalendar straight into XML: components, properties, parameters and values each become an element named in lowercase, so data can be converted to XML and back with the same semantic result.
tldr.outcome: Anyone who creates xCal following the RFC knows it can be converted to valid iCalendar. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 6868 and RFC 7529.

today: RFC 6321 is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 6868 and RFC 7529; it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why an XML Form of iCalendar
sections.content:
The iCalendar format (RFC 5545) is described in this RFC as a widely deployed interchange format for calendaring and scheduling data. It is specialized, though, and needs its own parser and generator. XML-based formats are widely used between applications, and the many XML tools make the data easier to work with.

xCal is defined as a straightforward mapping from iCalendar into XML. Data can be converted to XML and then back to iCalendar without losing any semantic meaning. Three design goals are stated: round-tripping gives the same semantic result as the starting point (all components, properties and parameters are preserved, except those that have default values); xCal preserves the semantics, so a full understanding of iCalendar is still required to modify or fully comprehend the data; and many extensions can be handled without updating this document.
sections.eli5: Think of the same story written in two languages. xCal is the second language for calendar events, and translating there and back gives you the same story.

sections.title: How iCalendar Maps to XML Elements
sections.content:
Before converting, iCalendar line folding MUST be undone and text escaping MUST be removed. A property with ENCODING set to BASE64 keeps its base64 data only if its value type is BINARY; otherwise the parameter is removed and the value is base64 decoded.

The whole stream sits in a root icalendar element in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:icalendar-2.0. Each iCalendar object, delimited by BEGIN:VCALENDAR and END:VCALENDAR, becomes a vcalendar element. Inside it, components live in a components element and properties in a properties element.

Names are mapped by one rule: the element has the same name as the iCalendar component, property or parameter, but in lowercase. So CALSCALE becomes calscale and the PARTSTAT parameter becomes partstat. The RFC says new components, properties and parameters added in the future are converted in the same way. Each property can hold a parameters element (which SHOULD NOT be present if empty) and one or more value elements.

Some cases are special. CATEGORIES, RESOURCES, FREEBUSY, EXDATE and RDATE hold several value elements. GEO becomes latitude and longitude elements. REQUEST-STATUS becomes code, description and optionally data. The VALUE parameter is dropped, because the value type is expressed by which value element appears.
sections.eli5: Every part of the calendar gets its own labeled box, and the label is just the old name in small letters. Boxes go inside bigger boxes, like a toy box holding smaller toy boxes.

sections.title: Value Types
sections.content:
Each iCalendar value type becomes an element named after the type in lowercase, such as text, boolean, integer, float, uri, duration, period and recur. A recur element holds child elements for the parts of the recurrence rule, for example freq, count, byday and bymonth.

The main difference in formatting is that dates, times and UTC offsets follow the syntax of XML Schema datatypes. Date components are separated by hyphens and time components by colons, so a date is written 2011-05-17, a date-time 2011-05-17T12:00:00 and a UTC offset -05:00. xCal does not use the XML Schema UTC offset in date-times; it keeps the iCalendar behavior of defining time zones through the TZID parameter.

Binary content is base64 data (per RFC 4648) in a binary element, where whitespace MAY be inserted to wrap lines and MUST be removed when converting back.
sections.eli5: Numbers, words, dates and yes/no answers each get their own kind of box. Dates are written with dashes and times with colons, the way XML likes them.

sections.title: Converting xCal Back to iCalendar
sections.content:
Going back, names SHOULD be converted to uppercase, since iCalendar names are case insensitive but common practice keeps them uppercase. Backslash character encoding and line folding MUST be applied as RFC 5545 requires, and non-binary value types MUST NOT be base64 encoded.

The skipped VALUE parameter is restored: when converting to iCalendar, it MUST be included if the value type is not the default for that property.
sections.eli5: To go back, you change the small-letter labels into capital letters again, put the lines in the old shape, and add any note the old style needed.

sections.title: Extensions and Unrecognized Properties
sections.content:
Extension properties and parameters with an X- prefix are mapped like any other: X-FOO becomes x-foo. Extension elements in the iCalendar namespace MUST begin with x-. Extensions in a different XML namespace SHOULD be kept in iCalendar through a new XML property, whose value is a single XML 1.0 element with a namespace declaration that MUST NOT be in the iCalendar namespace. Only extension elements that are immediate children of the properties element are converted. The order of XML properties is not preserved. If the XML cannot be held in a TEXT value it MUST be base64 encoded with ENCODING=BASE64 and VALUE=BINARY.

A converter may meet a property or parameter it does not recognize and so does not know its default value type. In that case the value is wrapped in an unknown element holding the unprocessed text, and converted back directly. This keeps the data intact.
sections.eli5: If a program finds a box it has never seen, it does not throw it away. It puts the contents in a plain wrapper marked unknown and hands it along untouched.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Because xCal is only a mapping from iCalendar, the RFC says no new security concerns arise related to calendar data; for those it points to Section 7 of RFC 5545. Using XML as a format does carry security risks, discussed in Section 7 of RFC 3470 and in the security discussion for the application/xml type in RFC 3023.
sections.eli5: Writing the calendar in XML does not make it any more dangerous than before, but XML has its own safety rules, and you should read them too.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC registers three things. The first is the XML namespace URN urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:icalendar-2.0. The second is the media type application/calendar+xml, with file extension xcs; it is an alternative for applications that use text/calendar, with optional parameters method, component and optinfo as defined for text/calendar, plus charset (use of utf-8 is STRONGLY RECOMMENDED). The third is the new iCalendar property XML, with status Current.
sections.eli5: The RFC puts three new names on the official list: a name tag for the XML words, a label for the file type, and a name for the special XML property.
